source.title: Bigger is not Always Better: Scaling Properties of Latent Diffusion Models
source.authors: K. Mei; Zheng-Zhong Tu; M. Delbracio; H. Talebi; Vishal M. Patel; P. Milanfar

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses language-model scaling laws as background, but its experiments concern latent diffusion image models and do not test the loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling results for image-generation metrics, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or fitted power-law relationships. Those image-model findings are recorded as related results under fits_no_version. It also cites language-model scaling work, which is not recorded as a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study scales latent diffusion image models and reports FID, CLIP and LPIPS against model size, training compute and sampling cost. It fits no power law and measures no held-out loss. It does not test V5's claim that the same power-law form holds beyond text, or any language-model version. LLM scaling laws appear only as related-work background.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Under identical sampling cost, smaller LDMs frequently outperform larger ones. This holds across samplers and after distillation, while larger models win when sampling constraints are relaxed. The authors also report that pretraining quality improves with training compute and drives downstream super-resolution quality. Claims are limited to the studied SD-style U-Net family.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales latent diffusion image models and evaluates image-generation metrics and inference cost; it does not use the language-model loss measurements or fitting procedure of the original scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Sampling budget and step count affect which model sizes perform better; CFG rate is selected separately by model and sampling steps. In super-resolution, the reported size advantage changes between ≤20 and >20 sampling steps.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 final text-to-image FID by size after 500K steps falls from 25.30 (39M) to 20.98 (866M). It is non-monotonic: 2B gives 22.15, worse than 866M, and 5B gives 20.14. No power law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this LDM family, text-to-image FID improves roughly with model size but not monotonically, and no power-law form is fitted.

fits_no_version.finding: Text-to-image FID and CLIP improve with training compute under moderate compute, with similar trends across sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this latent-diffusion family, generation metrics improve with training compute over the reported range.

fits_no_version.finding: Super-resolution FID depends more on model size than on fine-tuning compute, while LPIPS is most affected by compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In latent-diffusion super-resolution, the apparent scaling relationship depends on the quality metric.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed sampling cost, smaller models often achieve better FID. This holds across DDIM, DDPM and DPM-Solver++, and after distillation. In super-resolution it holds only at ≤20 steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size–quality relationship at fixed inference cost depends on sampling budget and task.

record.problems: The authors state that they did not conduct human evaluations, citing the many tested variants, and acknowledge that visual quality may differ from the quantitative metrics. The claims are specific to the studied LDM family; they identify other model families as future work. The text reports qualitative trends from figures but gives no uncertainty estimates for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Visual examples and supplementary comparisons are not separately recorded as rows because they do not provide a distinct quantitative result or explicit statement beyond the listed findings.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to larger runs.
Architecture shape effects at fixed parameter count. Only channel width is varied, and it changes the parameter count.
Power-law form in image diffusion models. Only qualitative metric trends with compute and size are reported, with no fit and no loss.
Predictable downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss in language models. The super-resolution fine-tuning results are image-model metric trends without a predictive fit.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on fitting choices.

missing.what: Final FID/CLIP per model size (39M–5B), non-monotonic at 2B (FID 22.15 vs 866M 20.98)
missing.versions: none (related to V5 only; no power-law fit)

record.verdict_notes: Image-generation metric trends, not loss power laws. No uncertainty estimates or human evaluation are reported. The supplement's guided-distillation results show inconsistent acceleration across sizes (Fig. 19).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal language-model parameter and token allocation.
Effects of language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds beyond text pretraining. The study measures image-generation metrics for latent diffusion models but does not test a power-law form.
Predictability of language-model downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting and setup choices.

rows.subject: scaled LDM family (39M–5B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and training compute; evaluated text-to-image generation.
rows.value: The paper reports that performance scales well with additional compute under moderate training resources, and that trends are similar across model sizes.
rows.note: This is a qualitative report about image-generation metrics, not held-out language-model loss or an explicit power-law fit.

rows.subject: scaled LDM family (83M–2B shown for super-resolution)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained, then fine-tuned for real-world super-resolution
rows.operation_detail: Compared super-resolution FID across model sizes and fine-tuning compute.
rows.value: The paper reports that super-resolution FID depends more on model size than on training compute, and that smaller models do not reach the performance of larger models regardless of training compute.
rows.note: The comparison concerns image-generation FID after downstream fine-tuning, not language-model loss.

rows.subject: scaled LDM family
rows.stage_stated: pretrained, then fine-tuned for real-world super-resolution
rows.operation_detail: Compared super-resolution LPIPS across training compute.
rows.value: The paper reports that training compute has the greatest impact on LPIPS, while noting inconsistencies between LPIPS and the generative metric FID.
rows.note: This is a reported image-restoration metric result, not a power-law test.

rows.subject: scaled LDM family (39M–5B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimal text-to-image FID at matched normalized sampling cost across model sizes.

conditions.value: DDIM; optimal CFG selected from tested rates

rows.baseline: larger models at the same sampling cost
rows.value: The paper reports that smaller models frequently outperform larger models across a range of sampling costs; the 83M model has the best FID at cost 3.
rows.note: The result concerns inference efficiency for image generation, not pretraining loss scaling.
